h1: SEO for preschools, where a parent decides within three kilometres
metaTitle: SEO for Preschools: Rank in the Parent's Radius
metaDescription: SEO for preschools and daycares in India. Win the tight local radius parents search in, with centre pages, safety content and reviews that ease worry.
answer: Nobody drives a three-year-old across a city twice a day. A preschool's realistic catchment is roughly two to three kilometres, or whatever sits on the parent's commute — so the entire SEO problem is being the most reassuring result inside a very small radius, during the November-to-February window when next year's admissions get decided.
takeaways: Your competition is the four or five centres in the same set of lanes, not every preschool in the city. Rankings change street by street, and a city-wide report tells you nothing useful.
Parents are not comparing curricula first. They're checking whether their child will be safe. **Staff ratio, background verification, CCTV access and washroom policy** are the content that converts.
Enquiries concentrate roughly November to February for a session starting in April or June. Content published in March is content published for next year.

For a franchise network, one page per centre with that centre's own staff, timings and photos — and a resolved answer on who owns each Google profile. Templated suburb pages are the fastest way to damage the whole domain.
Never publish a child's face or first name without written parental consent. It's the most common serious mistake on preschool websites and it has nothing to do with rankings.

sections.h2: Three kilometres, and why your city-wide ranking report is useless
body: Local results shift with the searcher's location. For most local businesses that's an inconvenience. For a preschool it's the entire market definition, because the decision is physically constrained: someone does the drop-off at 9am and the pick-up at 12.30, every weekday, with a toddler and a bag.

So `playschool near me` from one apartment complex and the same query from a complex 1.5 km away produce almost entirely different results, and both are correct. A report telling you that you rank fourth for `preschool in Pune` is measuring something no parent has ever searched.

Measure map-pack position from a grid of points across your actual catchment instead — where you're weak, in which direction, and whether that direction has a road people use. Two centres separated by a railway line are not competitors even at 800 metres apart, and no keyword tool knows that.
bullets: **`preschool near me` and `daycare near me`** — dominated by distance. You win these inside the ring and you cannot win them outside it, no matter what you publish.
**Locality name queries** — `playschool in Kondapur`, `daycare in Baner`, `preschool near Whitefield` — carry a wider effective radius and reward an actual page on your site.

**Landmark and complex queries** — `preschool near <apartment name>`, `playschool near <tech park>` — are low-volume, close to zero-competition and startlingly high intent. Write them for the landmarks your existing parents actually name.
**Full-day and timing queries** — `daycare with extended hours`, `creche near me open till 7pm` — working parents search by constraint, and most centres never mention their timings in indexable text.
**Age-ladder queries** — `playgroup vs nursery age`, `what age for LKG` — informational, but they're how a first-time parent enters the category.

callout.title: Don't build a page for every suburb
callout.body: The temptation with one centre is to publish `preschool in <twelve localities>`. Google reads near-identical location templates as scaled content and the demotion tends to hit the whole domain, not just those pages. Write locality pages for places you genuinely serve, and say honestly which centre serves them and how far it is.

sections.h2: Safety is the search, even when it isn't the query
body: A parent choosing a preschool is managing anxiety. That's the honest description of the buying state, and it shapes every page you write. Standalone preschools in India sit largely outside the school recognition framework in most states, so there's no accreditation a parent can look up. They check for themselves instead.

Almost none of what they check makes it onto preschool websites, which prefer a photograph of a colourful classroom and a paragraph about nurturing young minds. The centres that publish the specifics get the enquiry from the parent who has already read four other sites.

callout.title: Write the uncomfortable page
callout.body: A page titled 'How we handle the first two weeks of separation anxiety' will out-convert every marketing page on your site. It is the actual thing the parent is frightened of, nobody writes it, and it earns links from parenting forums and neighbourhood groups without any outreach at all.

body: Preschool enquiry volume has a clear shape. Interest builds from around October, peaks between November and February as parents lock in the next academic session, and drops sharply once term starts — with a smaller second wave for mid-year and daycare-only admissions. The session itself usually begins in April, or in June in states that work around the monsoon, so the calendar shifts a little by region.

Because the peak is a fixed annual event and Google needs time to trust a new page, everything commercial has to be live and indexed by roughly August or September. That means the quiet months are the working months, which is the opposite of how most centres budget.
numbered: **June to September — build.** Centre pages, locality pages, the safety content, the age-ladder explainers, the curriculum comparison. Get them indexed and settled while nobody is searching.
**October — tune the profile.** Photos refreshed, hours correct including the daycare extension, admission link live, Q&A seeded with the real questions about fees and timings.

**November to February — harvest and respond.** No new page builds. Speed of response is the ranking factor that matters now: enquiries in this window are being sent to four centres at once, and the first one to reply usually gets the visit.
**March to May — collect proof.** Annual day, graduation, the end of session. This is when parents are most willing to write a review and most willing to be quoted. Bank it for next cycle.

sections.h2: Reviews from parents, asked for without pressure
body: Reviews matter for local prominence and they matter more for the parent reading them. But a preschool's review ask is different from a restaurant's: you'll see this parent every single morning for the next two years, and a request that feels like pressure damages the relationship you're actually selling.
So the ask has to be genuinely low-stakes, well-timed and never repeated.
bullets: **Ask once, at a natural high point** — after annual day, after a parent-teacher meeting that went well, at the end of a session. Not in the first month, when the parent is still anxious.
**Make it easy and impersonal to complete.** A QR code on the newsletter or a link in the parent app beats a teacher standing there while you type.
**Never incentivise it.** A fee discount or a lucky draw for a review breaks Google's policy, gets swept in removals, and can take the profile with it.
**Never filter to only the happy ones.** Review gating is against policy, and a flawless 5.0 across 200 reviews reads as bought to exactly the sceptical parent you want.

**Reply to every review, and reply carefully.** Never name a child, never confirm a child attends, never discuss an incident publicly. 'Thanks — please do speak to our centre head directly' is the correct reply to a complaint.
**Take the negative one seriously in public.** A calm, specific, non-defensive reply to a bad review converts better than the four good ones above it.

callout.title: Photographs of children
callout.body: Written parental consent, per child, before any photo or video goes on the website, the Google profile or social media — and a documented way for a parent to withdraw it. Beyond the legal exposure, a site full of other people's children with no visible consent policy signals exactly the carelessness a parent is scanning for. Say on the site that you have a consent policy.

sections.h2: Curriculum comparison queries, and how to answer them honestly
body: `Montessori vs play way`, `what is play-based learning`, `Reggio Emilia vs Montessori`, `is Montessori good for a shy child`. These are among the most-searched preschool queries in India, and they're almost entirely answered by franchise marketing pages that conclude, remarkably, that the franchise's own method is best.

Write the honest version. Explain what each approach does, who it suits, and where yours is a genuine adaptation rather than a pure implementation — which for most Indian preschools it is. Saying so is more credible than claiming a purity nobody has.

Worth publishing too: 'Montessori' is used very loosely in India, with no single body policing the label, so a parent comparing three 'Montessori' centres may be comparing three different things. Being the centre that explains that, and states plainly what your teachers are actually trained in, wins the trust the comparison was searched for in the first place.

sections.h2: Franchise networks: one page per centre, and who owns the profile
body: For a chain the problem changes shape entirely. The brand ranks for the brand. The individual centre has to rank inside its own three kilometres, and usually can't, because the franchisor's site gives it a directory row with an address and a phone number. That thin centre page is the whole failure: nothing local to rank for the locality query, and nothing for the parent to read after they click out of the map pack.
bullets: **A real page per centre**, at a stable URL, with that centre's photos, its centre head named, its actual timings, its fee band, and directions from a landmark locals use.

**A separate Google Business Profile per centre**, with its own phone number and staffed hours. Decide in the franchise agreement who owns and controls it — this fight, discovered mid-dispute, has cost networks years of accumulated reviews.
**Point every profile at its centre page, never at the homepage.** It's the most common and most expensive misconfiguration in multi-location local SEO.
**Genuinely different content per centre.** Copy-pasting the same 300 words with the locality swapped is duplicate content at best and a scaled-content problem at worst.

**Watch for centres that filter each other.** Google generally shows one listing per business per query, so two centres 1.2 km apart compete rather than compound. Plan catchments before signing the lease.

**Give franchisees a locked template.** They will otherwise publish their own microsites, which then outrank or cannibalise the official centre pages. Our page on [local SEO services](/services/local-seo-services) covers how we structure this.

sections.h2: What it costs, and what we guarantee
body: A single-centre preschool is our ₹40,000 a month tier — one profile, one set of locality pages, a review habit and the safety content. A franchise network with twenty or more centres starts at ₹75,000, because it's twenty profiles, twenty pages and a cannibalisation map. Ex-GST, month-to-month after the first quarter. Full detail on [pricing](/pricing), and [what local SEO costs](/cost/local-seo-cost) covers the wider market.

The baseline we freeze on day one is your trailing-90-day count of qualified organic enquiries — calls, WhatsApp taps and form fills from parents asking about admission, tracked properly rather than guessed. Not sessions. A preschool site's session count is dominated by existing parents checking the holiday calendar, and we're not going to charge you for those.

Miss the baseline in 90 days and we keep working free until we beat it. We never promise a specific ranking position, because nobody controls Google's index and a business built on parents trusting you shouldn't buy marketing built on a claim that isn't true. Three clients a month is why we can carry that risk honestly.

callout.title: Fast surface, slow season
callout.body: Google Business Profile and review work is the fastest-moving surface in local SEO — four to eight weeks is common. The catch is the calendar: gains made in May don't get tested until November. If you start in the off-season, judge the work on map-pack position and profile actions first, and on admissions when the window actually opens.

faqs.q: How far do parents realistically travel for a preschool?
faqs.a: Usually two to three kilometres, or whatever falls on the daily commute. The drop-off happens twice a day with a small child, so distance beats almost every other factor. That means your competitive set is the handful of centres in the same lanes, and city-wide ranking reports measure a query nobody makes.

faqs.q: When should a preschool start SEO for the next admission season?
faqs.a: Around June to September for a November-to-February enquiry peak. Pages need to be live and indexed before demand arrives, and Google takes weeks to trust a new commercial page. Starting in December means paying for work that lands after most parents have already paid a deposit somewhere else.

faqs.q: What content actually converts a preschool enquiry?
faqs.a: Specifics about safety and routine, not curriculum marketing. Adult-to-child ratio by age group, staff verification and training, CCTV coverage and parent access, first-aid arrangements, pickup authorisation, the hour-by-hour daily schedule, and an honest page about handling the first two weeks of separation anxiety.

faqs.q: Can we offer a fee discount for a Google review?
faqs.a: No. Incentivised reviews break Google's policy, get removed in sweeps, and can jeopardise the whole profile. So does filtering the ask to only happy parents. Ask everyone, once, at a natural high point like annual day or a good parent-teacher meeting, and make it easy to ignore.

faqs.q: How should a preschool franchise structure its website?
faqs.a: One substantial page per centre at a stable URL, with that centre's own photos, staff, timings, fee band and directions — plus a separate Google Business Profile per centre pointing at that page rather than the homepage. Settle profile ownership in the franchise agreement, and give franchisees a locked template so they don't launch competing microsites.

faqs.q: Is it safe to put photos of children on our website?
faqs.a: Only with written parental consent for each child, and a documented way to withdraw it. This matters legally, and it matters commercially: a parent scanning your site for signs of carelessness will notice. Publishing your consent policy is itself a trust signal worth more than the photographs.
